name: Halverson & Obi Hall
description:
Halverson & Obi Hall sits on the corner of Reconstruction Row and Feeder Line 9 in the Circuit's Ward 14, a solidly working-class district known for its machine shops and water treatment workers. The building is a converted pre-megacity warehouse — three stories of exposed brick and reinforced steel, the original loading dock doors still operational and thrown open on warm nights to spill music into the street. The main floor holds 600 comfortably and has hosted the same weekly dance night, the Feeder Line Sessions, every Thursday for thirty-one consecutive years. The upper gallery is reserved for seated listening and has acoustic baffling that took a local collective of sound engineers eight years to perfect.

The hall is community-owned through a mutual trust established in 2194 by the Halverson-Ibarra and Obiechina families, both of whom worked the Feeder Line and wanted a space that couldn't be bought out from under the neighborhood. There is a strict no-corporate-sponsorship policy enforced by the trust's board, which has refused offers from Vantablack Media subsidiaries on four separate occasions. The kitchen operates every night the hall is open, and the tradition of feeding anyone who shows up regardless of ability to pay dates to the hall's founding. Notable events include the 2217 Circuit Requiem memorial concert, a six-hour community gathering following a fatal industrial accident that killed 34 Feeder Line workers, which drew over 2,000 people through multiple rotations.
creator: Halverson-Ibarra and Obiechina family collective, est. 2194
genre: Circuit folk, worker blues, polyrhythmic dance, traditional hybrid forms
audience: Circuit workers, trade union members, multi-generational neighborhood families, Tier 3 visitors seeking authentic Circuit culture, folk revival enthusiasts
cultural_impact: Halverson & Obi Hall is one of the most stable and beloved community institutions in the Circuit, representing a model of cultural infrastructure that resists corporate capture. Its no-sponsorship policy and community ownership have made it a template studied by other neighborhoods attempting to establish similar spaces. The Feeder Line Sessions have launched more Circuit folk careers than any other single venue in Meridian 88, and the hall's archives — recordings of every performance since 2194 — constitute an irreplaceable oral and musical history of Ward 14's working communities.
known_fans: Circuit folk musicians and their families
Tier 3 workers with roots in the Circuit
story_hooks: The Halverson & Obi trust board receives a legal challenge to the community ownership structure — a Vantablack subsidiary has found a loophole in a 2189 municipal zoning law that could void the original trust. They have 30 days to respond, and the hall's Thursday night regulars are not willing to let it go quietly.
A musician who left Ward 14 for the Spire fifteen years ago returns to play an unannounced set at the Feeder Line Sessions. Their presence reopens old wounds about who gets to leave and who stays.

Someone has been recording the hall's performances and selling bootleg neural feeds on the gray market. The trust wants to find them — but so does a Tier 5 collector who will pay a significant sum for access to the archives.
